# A reverse-Tom-Friedman moment.

My uber driver yesterday was an enterprising young Ethiopian woman in her early 30s who, with her husband, has built an independent transportation company with 6 vehicles, and employing 5 drivers, while raising 2 kids (Ethiopians dominate the rideshare business in Seattle and several are very enterprising). Very clever positioning too — she has a wheelchair capable van for eg. and a focus on medical transport needs. She showed me the website she built herself after taking a coding course several years ago, and is now trying to build an app. I was very impressed. Takes serious initiative to try to do direct-to-customer competition against rideshare, and come up with a competitive positioning etc. Then she said she was planning to build the app herself after a friend quoted like >10k for it. I assumed she meant with AI but she meant by hand.

That alarmed me. I told her a simple app like she had in mind shouldn’t cost more than a few hundred bucks in tokens now with AI, and she seemed both surprised by that estimate and expressed reluctance about doing it that way because she “didn’t trust AI”. Even though she uses ChatGPT and in fact had been chatting with it about the project and it had told her the quote was too high. But apparently it had only told her too high as a human estimate. It hadn’t suggested the coding agent option (?? shouldn’t default ChatGPT be up to speed on coding agent capabilities by now?)

This isn’t the only,y such example to cross my radar. I’ve encountered several smart and high-agency non-tech people who haven’t realized how easy and cheap things have gotten and are still pursuing slow and expensive technology plans. And mostly working within chat interfaces only, which limits AI to an advisory role with limited cut-and-paste agentic ability.

We seem to be at a dangerous moment where people who aren’t keeping up with frontier capabilities are at growing risk of spending far too much time and money on certain things. Especially people who can’t afford to. I imagine a small business with 6 car payments and 5 employees doesn’t have much margin for financial error.

It’s also making me wonder about how to update the old “everyone should learn to code” advice, which was good advice ~2000-2024 or so, even if all you could afford was a coding bootcamp of a couple of months. 

Now, rather dangerously, the anti-tech crowd is prematurely gloating that you no longer need to “learn coding” and that maybe it was never a good idea, and it’s time for a revenge of the humanities etc. That’s a dangerously not-even-wrong set of conclusions. 

*Telling people they can now safely avoid computer science education, or worse, that it is a liability, is the worst advice in the world right now.*

You now need go *beyond* learning coding to count as literate. The average person now needs to efficiently leapfrog as much of trad CS foundations knowledge as possible and get a bootcamp-grade education in using coding agents for straightforward needs. There’s a whole new fortune at the bottom of the code-demand pyramid. Simple websites, apps, automations etc. for small businesses representing tens of thousands in recurring revenue value. But also simple dashboards and business process tooling at the bottom of the enterprise pyramid worth millions, that will now be in-scope for non-tech spreadsheet-driving managers and execs (eg finance, HR type managers who were previously low-agency customers for code).

How much do you need to know? Clearly people like me (~ over 30 and with a technology background) are benefitting from both hands-on programming experience (rare in the future) and more importantly, being steeped in the conceptual universe of computing all the way down, with familiarity with the lingo. Makes it easy to supervise coding agents because even when you don’t know what to ask for, you probably know what you don’t know and whom to ask for help. We’re operating mostly in our known-unknown. But this is probably too much for future non-tech users of coding agents. You can probably unlock 80% of the fortune at the bottom of the pyramid with much less background. Harnesses for regular people can probably offer lots of templates etc., the way slide and docs apps now offer document templates.

But most people aren’t really ready for this. Coding agent capabilities are in their unknown unknown zone. They lack the conceptual vocabulary to appreciate what’s possible now. Which means a new kind of coding bootcamp is becoming necessary. You probably still need some [[75vdmatmmhxap7fxg8h05vqr3v | bike-riding training]] with hands-on exposure, but far less than before. You just need enough to move a lot of unknown-unknown into known-unknown. And you need a different flavor of conceptual education, perhaps with a greater emphasis on security and data persistence concepts. And a good deal more managerial basics, since you’re now supervising artificial programmers.
